newsitem.title: GERMANY: German analysts - high French deficit is major risk.
newsitem.headline: German analysts - high French deficit is major risk.

text.p: A French deficit as high as 3.8 percent of gross domestic product would pose a major risk to Europe's single currency project, German economists said on Thursday.

French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn on Thursday said France's budget deficit was likely this year to significantly overshoot the three percent of GDP target set down in the Maastricht Treaty.

German analysts said a French deficit level of 3.4 percent would not be disastrous for economic and monetary union (EMU), but a higher number than that would put serious strain on chances of launching the euro in January 1999.
BHF Bank chief economist Hermann Remsperger said: "If this is really a question of up to 3.8 percent, the country cannot in my view take part in monetary union.

"If it (the deficit) is significantly above 3.0 percent, it will undermine the stability pact. One cannot let a country with a deficit over 3.5 percent into currency union and then penalise it right away -- that just won't work."

Thomas Mayer, economist at Goldman Sachs, Frankfurt, said the issue of a 3.8 percent 1997 deficit would probably never arise because the French would have to pare the number down to have any chance of meeting EMU goals in 1998.
"Strauss-Kahn will have to make an effort to confine the deficit to 3.4 percent in order to reach 3.0 percent in 1998," Mayer said.

"Convergence demands a long-term consolidation of public finances. If a country is above 3.0 percent in 1998, then that is not consolidation and fines will have to be paid. Strauss-Kahn has in my view a strong incentive to bring the deficit down."
DB Research economist Werner Becker said a 3.8 percent French deficit would automatically exclude the country from monetary union, making a delayed launch of the euro a real probability.
"France has a choice -- either it manages 3.4 percent or less, then it is in, or the deficit goes out of control, and then it is out," Becker said.
"For political reasons, currency union without France would be damaging. The probability is very high that it will be postponed."
Ulrike Kastens, economist at Trinkaus Capital Management in Duesseldorf, was even more pessimistic.
"What Strauss-Kahn said today is a real blow. The year is nearly over. One can hardly do anything more to push the deficit down," Kastens said.
Dresdner Bank economist Jutta Kayser was one of the few optimistic voices.

"The statements (from Strauss-Kahn) cannot be viewed as a risk of a weakening of the convergence criteria. I believe (French Prime Minister Lionel) Jospin will take back some of its election promises and push though savings," she said.
"I think it is unlikely that France will have a 3.5 percent or 3.6 percent deficit, it will rather be a little better. Otherwise we will have a delay."
But some economists said currency markets were already factoring in the prospect of a soft euro.
"The currency markets show -- a weak currency union is on the way," said Remsperger.
